questions.prompt: For unweighted activity selection, which activity should a greedy algorithm choose first among those compatible with the current schedule?
options: The activity with the earliest finishing time
The activity with the earliest start time
The activity with the longest duration
The activity with the highest identifier
answer: The activity with the earliest finishing time
questions.explanation: Choosing the earliest finish leaves the largest remaining time interval for future compatible activities. This exchange choice is optimal for the unweighted problem.

questions.prompt: Activities have intervals [1,3], [2,5], [4,6], [6,8], and [7,9]. Using the earliest-finish-time rule and allowing an activity to start when the previous one finishes, how many activities are selected?
questions.explanation: Choose [1,3], then [4,6], then [6,8]. The intervals [2,5] and [7,9] conflict with a selected activity, so the maximum compatible set has size three.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the earliest-finish-time activity-selection algorithm are correct?
options: Sorting by finish time takes O(n log n)
A scan after sorting takes O(n)
The greedy choice is optimal for maximizing the number of unweighted activities
Choosing the longest activity first is always optimal
answer: Sorting by finish time takes O(n log n)
A scan after sorting takes O(n)
The greedy choice is optimal for maximizing the number of unweighted activities
questions.explanation: The algorithm sorts activities by finish time and takes each compatible one. The exchange argument proves optimality for count maximization; longest duration is not a safe rule.

questions.prompt: Activities are A=[0,10], B=[0,5], C=[5,10]. Which greedy choice maximizes the number of compatible activities?
options: Choose A, yielding one activity
Choose B then C, yielding two
Choose C then A, yielding two
All three are compatible
answer: Choose B then C, yielding two
questions.explanation: B finishes at time 5 and C starts at 5, so they are compatible under the stated endpoint convention. Choosing A prevents selecting either of them.

questions.prompt: A schedule contains activities finishing at times 4, 7, 9, and 12. The selected activity ends at time 7. How many listed activities remain compatible if their start times are 7, 8, 9, and 10 respectively?
questions.explanation: Each listed start time is at least 7, so all four activities are compatible with the previously selected activity under the convention that touching endpoints do not overlap.

questions.prompt: Why does sorting intervals by earliest finish time solve unweighted activity selection but not weighted activity selection in general?
options: The unweighted objective counts activities equally
A long high-value activity may outweigh several short activities in the weighted case
Weighted activity selection is solved by the same rule without modification
The weighted problem may require dynamic programming over compatible predecessors
answer: The unweighted objective counts activities equally
A long high-value activity may outweigh several short activities in the weighted case
The weighted problem may require dynamic programming over compatible predecessors
questions.explanation: Earliest finish maximizes the number of activities, not their total weights. Weighted intervals can make an early-finishing low-value activity inferior; dynamic programming compares taking an interval with skipping it.

questions.prompt: Fractional knapsack has capacity 50. Items have (value, weight) pairs (60,10), (100,20), and (120,30). What maximum value does the greedy value/weight rule obtain?
questions.explanation: The value densities are 6,5,4. Take the first two items for value 160 and weight 30, then 20/30 of the third for value 80; total value is 240.

questions.prompt: A fractional-knapsack item has value 84 and weight 12. What value density does it contribute?
questions.explanation: The value-to-weight ratio is 84/12=7 value units per weight unit.

questions.prompt: Why is sorting by value/weight ratio optimal for fractional knapsack but not for 0/1 knapsack?
options: Fractional items permit taking the remaining capacity proportionally
The 0/1 problem has no weights
The ratio is undefined for fractional items
0/1 items can always be divided into equal parts
answer: Fractional items permit taking the remaining capacity proportionally
questions.explanation: For fractional items, exchanging a lower-density portion for a higher-density one improves value until capacity is filled. The indivisibility in 0/1 knapsack prevents that exchange argument from guaranteeing an integral solution.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the greedy solution to fractional knapsack are correct?
options: Items are considered in nonincreasing value density
At most one selected item needs to be fractional
The algorithm may leave capacity unused even though a positive-value item remains
The method is optimal when item values and weights are positive
answer: Items are considered in nonincreasing value density
At most one selected item needs to be fractional
The method is optimal when item values and weights are positive
questions.explanation: The algorithm fills items in density order. It may take a fraction of the boundary item, after which capacity is full; positive-value items are not skipped while space remains.

questions.prompt: For 0/1 knapsack with capacity 10, items (value,weight) are A=(12,6), B=(10,5), C=(10,5). Which set has maximum value?
options: A only, value 12
B and C, value 20
A and B, value 22
A, B, and C, value 32
answer: B and C, value 20
questions.explanation: A weighs 6, so it cannot be paired with either weight-5 item. B and C together exactly fill capacity and yield value 20, exceeding A's value 12.

questions.prompt: A fractional knapsack has 18 units of capacity remaining. The next item has weight 24 and value 72. How much value is obtained by taking the maximum feasible fraction?
questions.explanation: The item density is 72/24=3. Taking 18/24=3/4 of it yields value 3×18=54.

questions.prompt: Which properties support a greedy-choice proof?
options: An optimal solution can be transformed to include the greedy choice without worsening it
The remaining subproblem has the same structure
A locally best choice is assumed optimal without proof
An exchange argument can compare a greedy solution with an optimum
answer: An optimal solution can be transformed to include the greedy choice without worsening it
The remaining subproblem has the same structure
An exchange argument can compare a greedy solution with an optimum
questions.explanation: Greedy correctness requires a proof that a safe local choice belongs to some optimum, then that the residual problem is solvable optimally. An unproved local intuition is insufficient.

questions.prompt: A greedy algorithm repeatedly chooses the locally cheapest edge to build a spanning tree, while avoiding cycles. Which algorithm is described?
options: Kruskal's algorithm
Dijkstra's algorithm
Bellman-Ford algorithm
Floyd-Warshall algorithm
answer: Kruskal's algorithm
questions.explanation: Kruskal processes edges in nondecreasing weight and adds an edge exactly when it connects different components, producing a minimum spanning tree.

questions.prompt: Kruskal's algorithm processes edges of weights 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order. The first edge is accepted, the second accepted, the third rejected because it closes a cycle, and the fourth accepted. What is the total accepted weight so far?
questions.explanation: The accepted edges have weights 1, 2, and 4. Their sum is 7; the weight-3 edge is rejected because it would create a cycle.

questions.prompt: Which facts about Kruskal's minimum-spanning-tree algorithm are correct?
options: Edges are considered in nondecreasing weight order
A disjoint-set structure can test whether endpoints are already connected
It may reject an edge that would create a cycle
It requires the graph to be directed
answer: Edges are considered in nondecreasing weight order
A disjoint-set structure can test whether endpoints are already connected
It may reject an edge that would create a cycle
questions.explanation: Kruskal is a greedy algorithm for undirected graphs. Sorting edges and maintaining connected components with disjoint sets allows it to avoid cycles.

questions.prompt: In a connected weighted undirected graph, all edge weights are distinct. What can be concluded about its minimum spanning tree?
options: It is unique
It is always a path
It has the maximum total weight
It contains every edge
answer: It is unique
questions.explanation: Distinct edge weights eliminate ties in the cut/cycle choices that could lead to alternative optimal trees. A connected graph therefore has a unique MST.

questions.prompt: A connected graph has 9 vertices. How many edges does any spanning tree contain?
questions.explanation: Every tree on V vertices has V−1 edges. For V=9, a spanning tree contains 8 edges.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe the cut property for a minimum spanning tree?
options: A minimum-weight edge crossing a cut is safe for some MST
If the minimum crossing edge is unique, it belongs to every MST
The cut must contain exactly one vertex
An edge entirely within one side crosses the cut
answer: A minimum-weight edge crossing a cut is safe for some MST
If the minimum crossing edge is unique, it belongs to every MST
questions.explanation: The cut property states that a lightest edge crossing any cut can be included in an MST; uniqueness makes it mandatory. A cut partitions the vertices into two sets, and only edges between them cross it.

questions.prompt: Why does Kruskal reject an edge whose endpoints are already in the same disjoint-set component?
options: Adding it would create a cycle
Its weight must be negative
It would disconnect the graph
The edge must be directed
answer: Adding it would create a cycle
questions.explanation: The endpoints are already connected by selected edges. Adding another edge between them closes a cycle and cannot be necessary for a spanning tree.

questions.prompt: A tree has 12 vertices. What is the number of edges accepted by Kruskal before a spanning tree is complete?
questions.explanation: A spanning tree on 12 vertices has 12−1=11 edges. Kruskal stops once that many edges connect all vertices.

questions.prompt: Prim's algorithm grows a tree from a start vertex. Which edge does it choose at each step?
options: A minimum-weight edge with exactly one endpoint in the current tree
The globally heaviest edge not yet used
Any edge between two vertices outside the tree
The edge that creates the largest cycle
answer: A minimum-weight edge with exactly one endpoint in the current tree
questions.explanation: Prim maintains a cut between the current tree and remaining vertices, then adds the lightest crossing edge. This preserves the growing-tree invariant.

questions.prompt: Which statements comparing Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms are correct?
options: Both produce a minimum spanning tree on a connected undirected weighted graph
Prim grows one connected tree
Kruskal may maintain several forest components before completion
Neither can handle negative edge weights for an MST
answer: Both produce a minimum spanning tree on a connected undirected weighted graph
Prim grows one connected tree
Kruskal may maintain several forest components before completion
questions.explanation: Both algorithms rely on MST cut/cycle properties and work with negative weights. Prim grows a single tree; Kruskal builds a forest that merges components.

questions.prompt: A weighted connected graph has vertices A,B,C,D and edges AB=1, AC=4, BC=2, BD=5, CD=3. What is the total weight of its MST?
questions.explanation: Kruskal selects AB=1 and BC=2. Edge CD=3 connects D without a cycle, yielding a spanning tree of weight 1+2+3=6.

questions.prompt: A graph has two disjoint components. What does Kruskal produce after processing all edges?
options: A minimum spanning forest with one tree per component
A spanning tree connecting the components without an edge
No selected edges
A directed arborescence
answer: A minimum spanning forest with one tree per component
questions.explanation: No edge connects separate graph components, so a spanning tree of the entire graph is impossible. Kruskal returns a minimum spanning tree within each component, forming a forest.

questions.prompt: Which statements about minimum spanning trees are correct?
options: An MST minimizes total edge weight among all spanning trees
Every MST has exactly V−1 edges for a connected graph
An MST is necessarily a shortest-path tree from every root
Negative edge weights are allowed
answer: An MST minimizes total edge weight among all spanning trees
Every MST has exactly V−1 edges for a connected graph
Negative edge weights are allowed
questions.explanation: An MST optimizes total weight, not paths from a root. It has V−1 edges when the graph is connected, and negative edges do not invalidate the cut-based algorithms.

questions.prompt: For the graph with edges AB=2, AC=3, BC=1, and CD=4, find the total weight of its minimum spanning tree.
questions.explanation: Choose BC=1, AB=2, and CD=4. These three edges connect all four vertices without a cycle, with total weight 7.

questions.prompt: Dijkstra's greedy shortest-path algorithm is correct under which edge-weight condition?
options: All edge weights are nonnegative
All edge weights are strictly negative
The graph must be a tree
Every edge must have identical weight
answer: All edge weights are nonnegative
questions.explanation: With nonnegative weights, extending a path cannot make it shorter, so the smallest tentative distance is safe to finalize. Negative edges can invalidate this greedy choice.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Dijkstra's algorithm are correct?
options: It repeatedly finalizes the vertex with minimum tentative distance
It relaxes outgoing edges from a finalized vertex
It works correctly with negative edge weights in general
A binary heap implementation can achieve O((V+E)log V) time
answer: It repeatedly finalizes the vertex with minimum tentative distance
It relaxes outgoing edges from a finalized vertex
A binary heap implementation can achieve O((V+E)log V) time
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's invariant finalizes the closest unsettled vertex and relaxes adjacent edges. Negative edges can later improve a finalized distance; a binary heap gives the stated common bound.

questions.prompt: Why can Dijkstra's algorithm fail with negative edge weights?
options: A vertex finalized early may later receive a shorter path through a negative edge
Negative edges make the graph disconnected
The priority queue cannot store negative numbers
The algorithm requires every weight to be an integer
answer: A vertex finalized early may later receive a shorter path through a negative edge
questions.explanation: The greedy proof assumes path extensions cannot reduce cost. A negative edge can create a shorter route after a vertex was declared final, violating that invariant.

questions.prompt: In a graph with nonnegative edges, Dijkstra has tentative distances d(A)=4, d(B)=7, and d(C)=5 among unsettled vertices. Which distance value is finalized next?
questions.explanation: Dijkstra selects the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance. The minimum of 4, 7, and 5 is 4.

questions.prompt: Which statements about a greedy algorithm's proof are important?
options: The greedy choice must be shown safe
The remaining problem after the choice should preserve optimal substructure
A counterexample can refute a proposed greedy rule
Testing many examples proves correctness for all inputs
answer: The greedy choice must be shown safe
The remaining problem after the choice should preserve optimal substructure
A counterexample can refute a proposed greedy rule
questions.explanation: Correctness needs a general argument, often an exchange proof plus optimal substructure. A single counterexample disproves a rule, while finitely many successful tests cannot establish universal correctness.

questions.prompt: A greedy coin system uses denominations {1,3,4}. For amount 6, what does the largest-coin-first rule return, and what is the optimum number of coins?
options: Greedy 3 coins; optimum 2 coins
Greedy 2 coins; optimum 2 coins
Greedy 4 coins; optimum 3 coins
Greedy 3 coins; optimum 3 coins
answer: Greedy 3 coins; optimum 2 coins
questions.explanation: Greedy takes 4, then 1 and 1, for three coins. The optimal solution is 3+3, using two; thus the largest-denomination rule is not universally optimal.

questions.prompt: For denominations {1,5,10,25}, how many coins does the usual largest-coin-first method use to make 41?
questions.explanation: Take 25, then 10, then 5, then 1. This uses four coins total.

questions.prompt: Which statements about greedy coin change are correct?
options: Largest-denomination-first is optimal for every denomination system
It is optimal for some canonical coin systems
A counterexample system can show the rule is not universally correct
Dynamic programming can solve the general minimum-coin problem
answer: It is optimal for some canonical coin systems
A counterexample system can show the rule is not universally correct
Dynamic programming can solve the general minimum-coin problem
questions.explanation: Greedy works for canonical systems such as standard currency in many settings, but not all sets of denominations. Dynamic programming provides a general solution for positive integer denominations.

questions.prompt: In Huffman coding, which two symbols are combined at each construction step?
options: The two least frequent symbols or subtrees
The two most frequent symbols
Any two symbols with equal frequency
The first two symbols alphabetically
answer: The two least frequent symbols or subtrees
questions.explanation: Huffman repeatedly merges the two lowest-frequency nodes into a parent whose weight is their sum. Repeating this greedy operation builds an optimal prefix-code tree.

questions.prompt: Huffman coding has symbol frequencies 5, 7, 10, and 15. What is the total weighted path length of the resulting code tree?
questions.explanation: Merge 5+7=12, then 10+12=22, then 15+22=37. The total weighted path length equals the sum of merge weights: 12+22+37=71.

questions.prompt: Which properties hold for a Huffman code?
options: It is prefix-free
More frequent symbols receive codewords no longer than less frequent ones in an optimal construction
It minimizes weighted external path length among binary prefix codes
Every symbol must receive the same codeword length
answer: It is prefix-free
More frequent symbols receive codewords no longer than less frequent ones in an optimal construction
It minimizes weighted external path length among binary prefix codes
questions.explanation: Huffman produces a binary prefix tree with minimum frequency-weighted code length. Codeword lengths vary with frequency; high-frequency symbols can be placed closer to the root.

questions.prompt: A Huffman tree has leaf frequencies 2, 3, and 7. The first merge combines 2 and 3. What is the total weighted path length after attaching the resulting weight-5 node with the weight-7 node?
questions.explanation: The two merges have weights 5 and 12. Summing these internal-node weights gives total weighted path length 17.

questions.prompt: An optimal merge pattern combines files of sizes 2, 3, 7, and 8. What is the minimum total merge cost?
questions.explanation: Merge 2+3=5, then 5+7=12, then 8+12=20. The sum of merge costs is 5+12+20=37.

questions.prompt: The optimal merge pattern for files uses the same greedy rule as Huffman coding. Which pair should be merged first?
options: The two smallest files
The two largest files
The smallest and largest files
Any two files
answer: The two smallest files
questions.explanation: Merging small files early keeps their data from being repeatedly included in large later merge costs. A min-priority queue efficiently selects the two smallest sizes.

questions.prompt: Which statements about greedy algorithms and matroids are correct?
options: For a matroid, sorting elements by weight and greedily adding independent elements yields an optimal basis
The exchange property supports the greedy-choice proof
Every optimization problem forms a matroid
Matroids provide a framework for identifying when greedy selection is optimal
answer: For a matroid, sorting elements by weight and greedily adding independent elements yields an optimal basis
The exchange property supports the greedy-choice proof
Matroids provide a framework for identifying when greedy selection is optimal
questions.explanation: Matroid independence and exchange properties guarantee that a weight-ordered greedy algorithm finds an optimal basis. Not every optimization problem satisfies the matroid axioms.

questions.prompt: Job sequencing with deadlines assumes each job takes one unit of time and yields profit only if completed by its deadline. Which greedy rule is standard?
options: Process jobs by decreasing profit, placing each in the latest available slot before its deadline
Process jobs by increasing deadline and ignore profit
Place every job in the earliest slot regardless of deadline
Choose the longest job first
answer: Process jobs by decreasing profit, placing each in the latest available slot before its deadline
questions.explanation: The algorithm considers higher-profit jobs first and assigns each to the latest free slot that meets its deadline, preserving earlier slots for jobs with tighter deadlines.

questions.prompt: Three unit-time jobs have (deadline,profit): A=(2,50), B=(1,40), C=(2,30). Using profit-descending job sequencing, what maximum total profit is scheduled?
questions.explanation: Schedule A in slot 2 and B in slot 1. C cannot be added because both slots through its deadline are occupied; the total profit is 50+40=90.

questions.prompt: Which assumptions are used by the standard job-sequencing greedy algorithm?
options: Each job takes one unit of time
Each job has a deadline and profit
A job earns its profit only if completed by its deadline
Jobs may have arbitrary processing times without changing the method
answer: Each job takes one unit of time
Each job has a deadline and profit
A job earns its profit only if completed by its deadline
questions.explanation: The classic greedy proof assumes unit-time jobs with deadlines and all-or-nothing profit. Arbitrary processing times alter feasibility and require different scheduling methods.

questions.prompt: For interval scheduling with weights, intervals A=[0,2] weight 3, B=[2,4] weight 3, and C=[0,4] weight 7 are given. Which schedule is optimal?
options: Choose A and B, total weight 6
Choose C, total weight 7
Choose all three, total weight 13
Choose A only, total weight 3
answer: Choose C, total weight 7
questions.explanation: A and B are compatible and total 6, while C conflicts with both and has weight 7. The maximum-weight schedule therefore selects C, showing count-based earliest finish is not enough.

questions.prompt: A graph has edge weights 1, 2, 2, 4 and vertices connected so that Kruskal selects the first three without cycles. What is the total weight of the resulting spanning tree?
questions.explanation: The accepted weights are 1, 2, and 2. Their sum is 5; the fourth edge is unnecessary once three vertices are connected.

questions.prompt: Which statements use the cycle property of minimum spanning trees?
options: A unique maximum-weight edge on a cycle belongs to no MST
A maximum-weight edge on a cycle can be omitted from some MST
Every minimum-weight edge on a cycle must be excluded
The cycle property can justify rejecting an edge
answer: A unique maximum-weight edge on a cycle belongs to no MST
A maximum-weight edge on a cycle can be omitted from some MST
The cycle property can justify rejecting an edge
questions.explanation: If an edge is the unique heaviest on a cycle, replacing it with a lighter cycle edge reduces tree cost. A non-unique maximum may be excluded from some MST, but minimum cycle edges need not be excluded.

questions.prompt: A connected graph has a cut with a unique lightest crossing edge e. What must be true of e?
options: It belongs to every minimum spanning tree
It belongs to no minimum spanning tree
It is the globally heaviest edge
It is a self-loop
answer: It belongs to every minimum spanning tree
questions.explanation: By the cut property, the unique minimum-weight edge crossing a cut is safe and must be included in every MST.

questions.prompt: A minimum spanning tree algorithm processes 10 vertices in a connected graph. How many successful edge additions are required?
questions.explanation: A spanning tree on 10 vertices has V−1=9 edges. Kruskal or Prim adds exactly that many edges.

questions.prompt: A greedy algorithm for selecting a maximum set of nonoverlapping intervals sorts by start time. Which counterexample pattern can make this rule fail?
options: One early-starting interval is very long and blocks several short compatible intervals
All intervals are pairwise disjoint
There is only one interval
All intervals have identical start and finish times
answer: One early-starting interval is very long and blocks several short compatible intervals
questions.explanation: An early start does not imply an early finish. Choosing a long interval can prevent selecting multiple shorter activities, whereas earliest-finish ordering preserves more remaining time.

questions.prompt: Which greedy choices are optimal for their stated classical problems?
options: Earliest finish time for maximum-cardinality unweighted activity selection
Maximum value/weight ratio for fractional knapsack
Minimum edge crossing the current cut for Prim's MST growth
Largest denomination for every arbitrary coin system
answer: Earliest finish time for maximum-cardinality unweighted activity selection
Maximum value/weight ratio for fractional knapsack
Minimum edge crossing the current cut for Prim's MST growth
questions.explanation: These rules have proofs under their stated assumptions. Greedy coin choice is not optimal for all denomination systems, as {1,3,4} for amount 6 demonstrates.

questions.prompt: Fractional knapsack has capacity 10 and items (value,weight) (30,5), (40,10), and (20,4). What value is obtained by the value-density greedy rule?
questions.explanation: The densities are 6, 4, and 5. Take the first item for value 30 and weight 5, then take the third item for value 20 and weight 4. The remaining capacity is 1, filled with one tenth of the second item for value 4; total value is 54.

questions.prompt: A fractional knapsack has 5 units of capacity left. The next item has value 50 and weight 10. What additional value is obtained by taking the remaining capacity fraction?
questions.explanation: The item's density is 50/10=5. Taking half the item uses five units and yields value 25.

questions.prompt: Which properties make fractional knapsack amenable to the density-greedy rule?
options: Items can be divided fractionally
Value is additive across item fractions
Capacity is a single additive constraint
Each item must be selected wholly or not at all
answer: Items can be divided fractionally
Value is additive across item fractions
Capacity is a single additive constraint
questions.explanation: Divisibility lets the algorithm exchange lower-density weight for higher-density weight continuously. Additive values and one capacity constraint make the ratio ordering optimal; indivisibility changes the problem.

questions.prompt: Huffman coding merges frequencies 4 and 6, then merges their sum with frequency 9. What is the total weighted path length contribution of these two merges?
questions.explanation: The first merge contributes 4+6=10; the next contributes 10+9=19. Summing merge weights gives 29 total weighted path length for this three-leaf tree.

questions.prompt: For symbols with frequencies a=5, b=7, c=10, d=15, the first Huffman merge combines a and b. What is the next smallest node weight?
questions.explanation: The merged node has weight 5+7=12. The remaining weights are 10, 12, and 15, so the next smallest is 10.

questions.prompt: Which statements about prefix codes and Huffman trees are correct?
options: No codeword is a prefix of another in a prefix code
A binary tree's leaves can represent symbols
Huffman repeatedly merges two minimum weights
A prefix code must assign every symbol the same bit length
answer: No codeword is a prefix of another in a prefix code
A binary tree's leaves can represent symbols
Huffman repeatedly merges two minimum weights
questions.explanation: Prefix-free codewords correspond to leaves of a binary tree, with no symbol leaf above another. Huffman's greedy construction creates variable-length codewords based on frequencies.

questions.prompt: A set of frequencies has two equal minimum values during Huffman construction. What is true about choosing either one first?
options: Either tie choice can lead to an optimal prefix code, though codewords may differ
Only the alphabetically first symbol is valid
The algorithm must stop
The resulting code must have a unique bit string assignment
answer: Either tie choice can lead to an optimal prefix code, though codewords may differ
questions.explanation: Ties may yield different tree shapes or code assignments, but each minimum-weight merge is safe. The weighted path length remains optimal.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the cut property for a minimum spanning tree are correct?
answer: A unique lightest edge crossing a cut belongs to every MST
A lightest edge crossing any cut is safe to add to some MST
questions.explanation: The cut property justifies choosing a minimum-weight crossing edge; uniqueness makes it compulsory for every MST. It does not require equal-sized sides or globally distinct weights.
options: A unique lightest edge crossing a cut belongs to every MST
A lightest edge crossing any cut is safe to add to some MST
The property applies only when all edge weights are distinct
The cut must separate the graph into components of equal size

questions.prompt: Which statements about the optimal merge pattern are correct?
options: The two smallest files are merged first
The sum of all merge costs equals the weighted path length of the merge tree
A min-heap can maintain the available file sizes
Merging the two largest files first is always optimal
answer: The two smallest files are merged first
The sum of all merge costs equals the weighted path length of the merge tree
A min-heap can maintain the available file sizes
questions.explanation: Repeatedly combining the two smallest sizes minimizes total merge cost, and a min-heap supports these selections. The resulting internal sums equal each original file size multiplied by its depth.

questions.prompt: A graph has edge weights 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Kruskal accepts edges of weights 1, 2, and 4 and rejects 3 because it creates a cycle. Why can the process still form a spanning tree?
options: The accepted edges already connect the endpoints of edge 3, while edge 4 may connect another component
A rejected edge is automatically added later
Kruskal requires all edges to be accepted
Weights do not affect the process
answer: The accepted edges already connect the endpoints of edge 3, while edge 4 may connect another component
questions.explanation: Rejecting a cycle edge preserves acyclicity, not connectivity progress. A later edge can still join separate components; Kruskal completes when V−1 accepted edges connect the graph.

questions.prompt: A connected graph has 7 vertices. If a minimum spanning tree's edge weights sum to 31 and six edges are present, what is the mean edge weight?
questions.explanation: A spanning tree has six edges. Their mean weight is 31/6≈5.166666667.

questions.prompt: Prim's algorithm uses a binary heap and adjacency lists. What is a common time bound for a connected graph?
options: O((V+E)log V)
O(V²E)
O(E²)
O(log V)
answer: O((V+E)log V)
questions.explanation: Each vertex is extracted once and edge relaxations update heap priorities. With adjacency lists and a binary heap, the common bound is O((V+E)log V).

questions.prompt: Which statements distinguish a minimum spanning tree from a shortest-path tree?
options: An MST minimizes the sum of selected edge weights
A shortest-path tree preserves distances from a designated source
An MST necessarily gives shortest paths from every root
The two structures can differ on the same graph
answer: An MST minimizes the sum of selected edge weights
A shortest-path tree preserves distances from a designated source
The two structures can differ on the same graph
questions.explanation: MST and shortest-path objectives are different. An MST minimizes global edge sum, while a shortest-path tree preserves source distances; one structure need not satisfy the other's objective.

questions.prompt: A weighted graph has edges AB=2, AC=5, BC=1, BD=4, CD=3. What is the weight of a minimum spanning tree?
questions.explanation: Choose BC=1, AB=2, and CD=3. These connect all four vertices without a cycle and total 6.

questions.prompt: A proposed greedy algorithm for an optimization problem always returns a feasible solution. What additional property is still needed to claim it is correct?
options: A proof that its solution is optimal for every valid input
A fast implementation on one example
A sorted input
A larger test suite only
answer: A proof that its solution is optimal for every valid input
questions.explanation: Feasibility establishes that constraints are met, not that the objective is maximized or minimized. A correctness proof must show optimality for all inputs in the problem domain.

questions.prompt: Which are common proof techniques for greedy algorithms?
options: Exchange argument
Stays-ahead argument
Cut-and-cycle properties for spanning trees
Assuming the first greedy output is optimal
answer: Exchange argument
Stays-ahead argument
Cut-and-cycle properties for spanning trees
questions.explanation: Exchange and stays-ahead proofs formalize why greedy choices preserve an optimum. MST correctness uses cut and cycle properties; merely assuming optimality is not a proof.

questions.prompt: A set of activities selected by earliest finish has compatible intervals [1,2], [2,4], [4,5], [5,8], and [8,9]. How many activities are selected?
questions.explanation: Each activity begins at the prior activity's finish, so all five are mutually compatible under the stated endpoint convention.

questions.prompt: A weighted activity-selection instance has interval values and compatibility constraints. Which standard recurrence supports an optimal solution?
options: OPT(j)=max(OPT(j−1), w_j+OPT(p(j)))
OPT(j)=min(OPT(j−1), w_j+OPT(p(j)))
OPT(j)=w_j×OPT(j−1)
OPT(j)=OPT(j+1)+1
answer: OPT(j)=max(OPT(j−1), w_j+OPT(p(j)))
questions.explanation: For the j-th finish-sorted activity, either skip it or take its weight plus the best solution among compatible earlier activities up to p(j). The maximum of these choices is optimal.

questions.prompt: Which facts explain why earliest-start-time is not a correct universal greedy rule for maximum-cardinality activity selection?
options: An early-starting activity may have a very late finish
That long interval can block many shorter compatible activities
Earliest-finish time leaves more room for subsequent activities
Activities cannot be sorted by start time
answer: An early-starting activity may have a very late finish
That long interval can block many shorter compatible activities
Earliest-finish time leaves more room for subsequent activities
questions.explanation: Start time alone says nothing about how much remaining time an activity consumes. The earliest-finishing rule is safe because it minimizes the time occupied by the first selected activity.

questions.prompt: For activity selection, activities have intervals [1,4], [3,5], [0,6], [5,7], [3,9], [5,9], and [8,10]. What is the maximum number of mutually compatible activities?
questions.explanation: Selecting by earliest finish gives [1,4], then [5,7], then [8,10]. These three are compatible. No four can fit: after the earliest feasible choices, the remaining intervals leave insufficient time.

questions.prompt: In a fractional-knapsack tie, two items have equal value-to-weight ratios. What can be said about choosing either first?
options: Either order yields the same value for any amount of capacity allocated between them
Only the heavier item is optimal
The lighter item must be rejected
The algorithm becomes incorrect
answer: Either order yields the same value for any amount of capacity allocated between them
questions.explanation: Equal densities contribute the same value per unit weight. If only part of the tied group fits, selecting weight from either item gives the same total objective value, assuming divisibility.

questions.prompt: Which statements about greedy methods for 0/1 knapsack are correct?
options: Sorting by value/weight ratio is not always optimal
The problem has an optimal-substructure dynamic-programming solution
A ratio-based greedy choice may leave a poor combination of remaining weights
Fractional divisibility is the property that makes the density proof work
answer: Sorting by value/weight ratio is not always optimal
The problem has an optimal-substructure dynamic-programming solution
A ratio-based greedy choice may leave a poor combination of remaining weights
Fractional divisibility is the property that makes the density proof work
questions.explanation: Indivisible items can make a high-density choice block a better combination. Dynamic programming handles the capacity state; the fractional greedy exchange depends on taking partial items.

questions.prompt: A shortest-path problem has a negative edge but no negative cycle. Which algorithm can correctly solve single-source shortest paths in general?
options: Bellman-Ford
Dijkstra
Prim
Kruskal
answer: Bellman-Ford
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford accommodates negative edge weights and can detect reachable negative cycles. Dijkstra's greedy finalization is not generally correct with negative edges.

questions.prompt: In a graph, Dijkstra has finalized distance d(u)=7 and an edge (u,v) has weight 4. What candidate distance is considered for v during relaxation?
questions.explanation: Relaxation proposes d(u)+w(u,v)=7+4=11 for vertex v, replacing its tentative distance only if this candidate is smaller.

questions.prompt: Which conditions allow Dijkstra's algorithm to finalize vertices greedily?
options: Edge weights are nonnegative
The vertex selected has minimum tentative distance
Relaxation updates neighbors of finalized vertices
Negative edges are harmless if there are no negative cycles
answer: Edge weights are nonnegative
The vertex selected has minimum tentative distance
Relaxation updates neighbors of finalized vertices
questions.explanation: Nonnegative edges ensure no later path through an unsettled vertex can reduce the selected minimum. The absence of negative cycles alone does not make negative edges safe for Dijkstra.

questions.prompt: A set of jobs has unit processing time and deadlines. Why is the latest feasible slot used when placing a selected high-profit job?
options: It preserves earlier slots for jobs with tighter deadlines
It maximizes the job's processing time
It makes every later deadline infeasible
It avoids sorting jobs by profit
answer: It preserves earlier slots for jobs with tighter deadlines
questions.explanation: Placing a job as late as possible before its deadline leaves earlier positions available for jobs that may have less scheduling flexibility.

questions.prompt: Three unit-time jobs have profits 100, 80, and 60 with deadlines 1, 2, and 2 respectively. Using profit-descending scheduling, what total profit is obtained?
questions.explanation: Schedule the profit-100 job in slot 1 and the profit-80 job in slot 2. The third job cannot be added because both slots through its deadline are occupied, giving 180 total.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the greedy-choice property are correct?
options: It asserts that some optimal solution begins with a greedy choice
It can be established by an exchange argument
It is equivalent to saying every local optimum is global
It must be combined with a correct solution to the residual problem
answer: It asserts that some optimal solution begins with a greedy choice
It can be established by an exchange argument
It must be combined with a correct solution to the residual problem
questions.explanation: A safe greedy choice can be exchanged into an optimum, after which the remainder must be solved optimally. The property does not imply that arbitrary local optima are global optima.

questions.prompt: For a connected graph with distinct edge weights, Kruskal processes an edge e that is the unique minimum across a cut. What follows?
options: e is included in the unique MST
e is rejected because it is a cut edge
e is included only if it is a self-loop
The MST is not defined
answer: e is included in the unique MST
questions.explanation: The cut property makes the unique lightest crossing edge safe. With all edge weights distinct, the MST itself is unique, and this edge belongs to it.

questions.prompt: Huffman construction combines weights 2, 4, 6, and 8. What is the sum of the merge weights?
questions.explanation: The merges are 2+4=6, then 6+6=12, then 8+12=20. Their total cost is 6+12+20=38.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Huffman code lengths and frequencies are correct?
options: A more frequent symbol can be assigned a shorter codeword
Huffman construction is optimal for binary prefix codes
Codeword lengths may differ
The frequency-weighted average length is minimized
answer: A more frequent symbol can be assigned a shorter codeword
Huffman construction is optimal for binary prefix codes
Codeword lengths may differ
The frequency-weighted average length is minimized
questions.explanation: The greedy merges produce an optimal binary prefix code and minimize the weighted external path length. Frequently used symbols tend to be nearer the root, while lengths can vary.

questions.prompt: A candidate solution satisfies every constraint and has objective value 42. What additional evidence is needed to show it is optimal?
options: A proof that no feasible solution has a better objective value
A second feasible solution with value 42
A larger input size
A greedy choice at the first step
answer: A proof that no feasible solution has a better objective value
questions.explanation: Feasibility and a good objective value do not establish optimality. A proof must show that no other feasible solution improves on 42, for example using an exchange or lower-bound argument.

questions.prompt: An activity starts at time 12 and ends at time 17. The last selected activity ends at time 12. Is it compatible under the convention that start equal to finish is allowed? Answer 1 for compatible and 0 otherwise.
questions.explanation: The new activity starts exactly when the previous one finishes. Under the stated half-open or endpoint-compatible convention, it can be selected, so the answer is 1.

questions.prompt: Which are common greedy applications with established optimal greedy rules under their stated assumptions?
options: Fractional knapsack
Huffman coding
Minimum spanning tree construction
General 0/1 knapsack by value density
answer: Fractional knapsack
Huffman coding
Minimum spanning tree construction
questions.explanation: Density ordering is optimal for fractional knapsack, repeated minimum-frequency merges give Huffman coding, and cut/cycle properties justify MST algorithms. Value-density greedy is not generally optimal for 0/1 knapsack.

questions.prompt: A scheduling problem asks for the maximum number of mutually compatible intervals, with all activities having equal value. Which sorting key enables the standard greedy solution?
options: Nondecreasing finishing time
Nondecreasing interval length
Nonincreasing starting time
Nonincreasing activity identifier
answer: Nondecreasing finishing time
questions.explanation: Selecting the earliest-finishing compatible activity is the safe greedy choice for maximum-cardinality interval scheduling.

questions.prompt: A fractional-knapsack item has value 90 and weight 15. If 40% of the item is selected, what value is gained?
questions.explanation: The value scales linearly with the selected fraction: 0.4×90=36.

questions.prompt: A graph has edges AB=1, BC=2, AC=3. Which edge does the cycle property allow an MST algorithm to discard?
options: AC with weight 3
AB with weight 1
BC with weight 2
No edge can be discarded
answer: AC with weight 3
questions.explanation: The triangle is a cycle and AC is its unique heaviest edge. It cannot belong to an MST because replacing it with a lighter edge reduces total weight.

questions.prompt: Which statements about interval compatibility are correct when intervals are half-open [s,f)?
options: An activity starting at the previous finish time is compatible
Two intervals with positive-length overlap are incompatible
The endpoint convention should be stated for boundary cases
Intervals touching at an endpoint necessarily overlap
answer: An activity starting at the previous finish time is compatible
Two intervals with positive-length overlap are incompatible
The endpoint convention should be stated for boundary cases
questions.explanation: Half-open intervals exclude their finish endpoint, so [a,b) and [b,c) do not overlap. Explicitly defining the convention avoids ambiguity in scheduling decisions.

questions.prompt: A minimum spanning tree on 6 vertices has total weight 42. What is its average edge weight?
questions.explanation: The tree has 6−1=5 edges. Dividing total weight by edge count gives 42/5=8.4.

questions.prompt: A graph's unique lightest edge is a self-loop. Can it belong to a minimum spanning tree?
options: No, a self-loop never helps connect distinct vertices
Yes, because it is the lightest edge
Only if the graph is directed
Only when all other edges are negative
answer: No, a self-loop never helps connect distinct vertices
questions.explanation: A spanning tree is acyclic and connects vertices. A self-loop creates a cycle of length one and adds no connectivity, so it is never included in an MST.

questions.prompt: Which characteristics distinguish a greedy algorithm from a dynamic-programming algorithm?
options: A greedy method commits to a locally safe choice without revisiting it
Dynamic programming compares alternatives across subproblems
A greedy method always works without proof
Dynamic programming may store results for overlapping subproblems
answer: A greedy method commits to a locally safe choice without revisiting it
Dynamic programming compares alternatives across subproblems
Dynamic programming may store results for overlapping subproblems
questions.explanation: Greedy algorithms commit to choices backed by a safety proof. Dynamic programming systematically combines alternatives and often caches overlapping states; neither paradigm is correct automatically.

questions.prompt: A job-sequencing schedule accepts three unit-time jobs with profits 18, 11, and 7. What is the total scheduled profit?
questions.explanation: The total profit is 18+11+7=36 for the three scheduled jobs.

questions.prompt: A greedy algorithm for a matroid sorts elements by increasing cost and builds a minimum-cost basis. Which elements are added?
options: An element is added if it preserves independence
Every element is added in sorted order
An element is added only if it creates a dependent set
Only the maximum-cost element is considered
answer: An element is added if it preserves independence
questions.explanation: The matroid greedy algorithm scans elements by weight and accepts one whenever the current set remains independent. It stops when a basis is formed.

questions.prompt: Which statements about greedy counterexamples are correct?
options: One valid counterexample disproves a universal optimality claim
A counterexample should satisfy the problem's assumptions
A counterexample proves every greedy algorithm fails
A counterexample can expose a missing assumption
answer: One valid counterexample disproves a universal optimality claim
A counterexample should satisfy the problem's assumptions
A counterexample can expose a missing assumption
questions.explanation: A counterexample must be within the stated domain and demonstrate failure of the claim. It refutes that rule's universal guarantee but says nothing about unrelated greedy algorithms.

questions.prompt: Why does Kruskal's algorithm use a disjoint-set union structure?
options: To detect whether an edge's endpoints are already connected by selected edges
To sort vertices by their degree
To compute shortest paths
To assign edge weights
answer: To detect whether an edge's endpoints are already connected by selected edges
questions.explanation: Find operations identify each endpoint's current component. If the representatives differ, Kruskal can safely add the edge and union the components; otherwise it would form a cycle.

questions.prompt: A connected graph with 15 vertices is processed by Kruskal. How many edges are rejected if the graph has 30 edges and the final spanning tree uses 14?
questions.explanation: Kruskal accepts 14 edges for the spanning tree. It rejects the other 30−14=16 edges as cycle-forming or unnecessary.

questions.prompt: An interval-scheduling greedy algorithm sorts by finish time. After selecting an interval ending at f, which candidates remain eligible?
options: Intervals with start time at least f
Intervals with finish time at most f
All intervals regardless of overlap
Only intervals that start before f
answer: Intervals with start time at least f
questions.explanation: A future activity is compatible when it begins no earlier than the finish of the last selected activity, under the stated nonoverlap convention.

questions.prompt: Which statements summarize when a greedy strategy is justified?
options: A locally optimal choice must be proven safe for an optimal solution
The residual problem should preserve the original optimization structure
An exchange or cut argument can establish correctness
A good result on sample inputs is a sufficient proof
answer: A locally optimal choice must be proven safe for an optimal solution
The residual problem should preserve the original optimization structure
An exchange or cut argument can establish correctness
questions.explanation: Greedy correctness requires a safe-choice argument and optimal substructure for the remaining instance. Examples may illustrate behavior, but only a general proof establishes the guarantee.
